title: Two Pointers, Sliding Windows and Prefix Sums
objectives: Build a prefix-sum array and answer range-sum queries in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing
Apply converging two pointers to pair-finding problems on sorted data in O(n)
Maintain fixed-window aggregates (sum, VWAP, max) in O(1) amortised time per step
Recognise when a naive O(nk) recomputation can be replaced by an incremental update
motivation: A desk needs the 50-tick rolling VWAP of a futures contract recomputed on every trade, plus every pairwise lot match between buy and sell flow. Recomputing each window from scratch costs O(nk) per day and blows the latency budget; the techniques in this lesson make every step O(1) amortised. These three patterns, prefix sums, two pointers, sliding windows, are the bread and butter of time-series processing and of quant interviews.

blocks.text: Prefix sums: pay once, query free

blocks.md: A **prefix-sum** array stores running totals: $\text{pref}[i]$ is the sum of the first $i$ elements, built in one $O(n)$ pass. Its superpower is that any contiguous range sum becomes a subtraction: $\sum_{j=\text{lo}}^{\text{hi}-1} a_j = \text{pref}[\text{hi}] - \text{pref}[\text{lo}]$, answered in $O(1)$. Cumulative PnL, cumulative volume and cumulative return series are all prefix sums, and they set up both sliding windows and two-pointer tricks later in this lesson.

blocks.code:
prices = [8, 5, 12, 9]
pref = [0]
for p in prices:
    pref.append(pref[-1] + p)
# pref = [0, 8, 13, 25, 34]

def range_sum(lo, hi):          # sum of prices[lo:hi]
    return pref[hi] - pref[lo]

print(range_sum(1, 3))          # 5 + 12 = 17
print(range_sum(0, 4))          # whole list = 34
blocks.caption: One O(n) pass buys unlimited O(1) range-sum queries.

blocks.text: Two pointers: converging on a pair

blocks.md: On a **sorted** array, two indices that start at the ends and move inward solve pair-finding in $O(n)$: if the pair sum is too small, only advancing the left pointer can help; if too large, only retreating the right pointer can. Every step eliminates one element from consideration forever, so the total work is linear, a proof by the shrinking window, the same invariant discipline as binary search. The same idea powers slow/fast pointer cycles and merging sorted trade and quote streams by timestamp.

blocks.code:
# Count pairs of order sizes (lots) that sum to the target clip
count_pairs = 0
target = 500
sizes = [100, 150, 350, 400]    # already sorted
i, j = 0, len(sizes) - 1
while i < j:
    s = sizes[i] + sizes[j]
    if s == target:
        count_pairs += 1
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    elif s < target:
        i += 1
    else:
        j -= 1
print(count_pairs)              # 2: (100,400) and (150,350)
blocks.caption: Converging pointers: each step permanently retires one element.

blocks.text: Sliding windows: O(1) updates instead of O(k) recomputation

blocks.md: A **fixed-size sliding window** over a stream recomputes a statistic on every step. The naive way re-sums all $k$ entries per step, $O(nk)$ overall. But when the window slides by one, one element enters and one leaves, so sums, products and VWAP components can be updated incrementally in $O(1)$ per step, $O(n)$ overall. The **rolling VWAP** (volume-weighted average price) is the canonical trading example: keep the window's $\sum p_i q_i$ and $\sum q_i$ and divide on demand.

blocks.title: Worked example: rolling 2-tick VWAP
items: Two subtractions and two additions replaced a full re-sum: the O(1)-per-step idea.

blocks.code:
from collections import deque

ticks = [(100.0, 200), (101.0, 100), (99.5, 300), (100.5, 100)]
k = 2
window = deque()
pv_sum = vol_sum = 0.0
for px, qty in ticks:
    window.append((px, qty))
    pv_sum += px * qty          # element enters
    vol_sum += qty
    if len(window) > k:         # element leaves
        old_px, old_qty = window.popleft()
        pv_sum -= old_px * old_qty
        vol_sum -= old_qty
    if len(window) == k:
        print(round(pv_sum / vol_sum, 4))
blocks.caption: Rolling VWAP: one enter, one leave, one division. Prints 100.3333, 99.875, 99.75.

blocks.md: **Variable-size windows** grow the right end while a condition fails and shrink the left end while it holds, for example, the longest run of ticks whose cumulative return stays under a threshold. Each pointer only ever moves forward, so the amortised cost is $O(n)$ even though a single step may scan several elements. For window **maxima**, sums are not enough: a monotone deque keeps candidate indices in decreasing value order, giving $O(1)$ amortised updates, you will implement it as a drill in the quant-algorithms phase.

blocks.caption: A simulated price stream: imagine maintaining a rolling 20-tick VWAP over it, one enter and one leave per tick.

blocks.title: Numerical drift in long-running windows
blocks.md: Incremental add/subtract accumulates floating-point rounding over millions of updates. Production rolling statistics periodically recompute the window aggregates from scratch (or use Kahan summation) to cap the drift, cheap insurance for a statistic that feeds execution decisions.

guidedExercise.prompt: Using the ticks $t_1 = (100.0, 200)$, $t_2 = (101.0, 100)$, $t_3 = (99.5, 300)$, $t_4 = (100.5, 100)$, compute the rolling 2-tick VWAP for each of the three windows by hand, showing $\sum pq$ and $\sum q$ at each step.
hints: Window 1 is $\{t_1, t_2\}$; window 2 is $\{t_2, t_3\}$; window 3 is $\{t_3, t_4\}$.
Update incrementally: subtract the departing tick's $p q$ and volume, add the arriving tick's.

independentExercise.prompt: (a) Trade volumes by minute are $[200, 100, 300, 100]$. Using a prefix-sum array, compute the total volume of minutes 2 through 4 (inclusive, 1-indexed) with a single subtraction. (b) Sorted order sizes $[100, 150, 350, 400]$ lots: how many pairs sum to exactly 500 lots? Trace the two-pointer method.
hints: Start pointers at both ends; a sum of 500 records the pair and retires both ends.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $\text{pref} = [0, 200, 300, 600, 700]$; minutes 2..4 give $\text{pref}[4] - \text{pref}[1] = 700 - 200 = 500$ lots. (b) $i=0, j=3$: $100+400=500$ - count 1, advance both. $i=1, j=2$: $150+350=500$ - count 2, pointers cross. Answer: **2 pairs**, in 3 loop iterations.

commonMistakes: Recomputing the whole window each step ($O(nk)$) when an enter/leave update would do ($O(n)$).
Off-by-one in prefix sums: $\sum_{j=\text{lo}}^{\text{hi}-1} a_j = \text{pref}[\text{hi}] - \text{pref}[\text{lo}]$, not $\text{pref}[\text{hi}+1] - \text{pref}[\text{lo}]$.
Using two pointers on an *unsorted* array for pair sums, the convergence argument needs sorted order.
Letting a fixed window's deque exceed length $k$ before popping, which leaves stale elements inflating the sums.
Dividing rolling VWAP by the wrong denominator: it is the window's $\sum q_i$, not the window length.
realWorldApplication: Analytics dashboards compute rolling averages, rolling volatility and moving ranges with exactly these incremental updates; database systems build prefix-sum (cumulative) columns for fast range reporting.
quantFinanceApplication: Rolling VWAP and rolling windows of returns/volume are computed tick-by-tick in execution algorithms; the O(1) enter/leave update is what makes it feasible at tick rate.
summary: Prefix sums cost $O(n)$ to build and make every range sum an $O(1)$ subtraction: $\text{pref}[\text{hi}] - \text{pref}[\text{lo}]$.
Two converging pointers on sorted data solve pair problems in $O(n)$ because each step permanently retires one element.
Fixed sliding windows update aggregates with one enter and one leave per step: $O(n)$ total instead of $O(nk)$.
Rolling VWAP maintains $\sum p_iq_i$ and $\sum q_i$ over the window and divides on demand.
Long-running incremental sums accumulate floating-point drift; periodic recomputation from scratch caps it.

quiz.prompt: Ticks: $t_1 = (100.0, 200)$, $t_2 = (101.0, 100)$. What is the 2-tick rolling VWAP over this window, to 4 decimal places?
Maintaining the maximum of a fixed window of size $k$ over $n$ ticks with a monotone deque costs, in total:
options: $O(nk)$, because each maximum needs a fresh scan
$O(n \log k)$, because the deque must stay sorted
$O(n)$ amortised, since each index is pushed and popped at most once
quiz.explanation: Every index enters the deque once and leaves at most once, so the total work across all steps is $O(n)$, i.e. $O(1)$ amortised per tick.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences, why does a prefix-sum array allow O(1) range-sum queries?
quiz.modelAnswer: Because sums are associative and additive, the sum of any contiguous range factors as the difference of two running totals: pref[hi], pref[lo]. Building pref once in O(n) makes every later query a subtraction.
quiz.explanation: Additivity of summation means the range sum telescopes into two prefix totals, so preprocessing buys constant-time queries.

quiz.prompt: Which of these tasks fit the sliding-window (incremental enter/leave) pattern?
options: Rolling VWAP over the last $k$ ticks
All-pairs shortest paths in a graph
Counting pairs in a sorted array with converging pointers
quiz.explanation: Fixed-window aggregates and sorted-array pair counting both retire one element and admit one per step. All-pairs shortest paths is a graph problem unrelated to windows.

flashcards.front: Range sum from a prefix-sum array
flashcards.back: $\sum_{j=lo}^{hi-1} a_j = pref[hi] - pref[lo]$ - an O(1) query after an O(n) build.

flashcards.front: Why do converging two pointers run in O(n)?
flashcards.back: Each step retires one element permanently (left advances or right retreats), so there are at most n steps in total.
On slide: pv_sum += p_in * q_in, p_out * q_out; vol_sum += q_in, q_out; VWAP = pv_sum / vol_sum.

flashcards.front: A rolling sum drifts after millions of updates. What is happening and what is the fix?
flashcards.back: Floating-point rounding accumulates across incremental add/subtract cycles. Periodically recompute the window aggregate from scratch (or use compensated/Kahan summation).
